21256-travels-through-the-south-of-franc:
Lieutenant-Colonel Pinkney of the North American Native Rangers travelled through southern France in 1807 and 1808. His route, he says, was never performed before: along the banks of the Loire, the Isère, and the Garonne. He travelled with the French government's permission. His book appeared in London in 1809.

He sails from Baltimore to Liverpool, crosses to Calais, buys a Norman horse, and posts south through Boulogne. Markets, prices, cottages, dances on the green, and French domestic economy fill his chapters. An American officer's view of Napoleonic France, written for English readers curious about the enemy's country, is the book's special value.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-stra: This article covers Strahov, the Prague abbey of the White Canons. Its library glows with Baroque gold. Joseph Sinkmajer gives its history. Bohemia's pride on the hill. Its gallery holds saints painted by Bohemian masters. Its stair hall frescoes dazzle every visitor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-martinov: This 1913 reference article on Martinov — the Jesuit of Russia. John Hungerford Pollen recounts his exiled years. His zeal served the scattered flock. The order prized its fearless son. The nineteenth century told his tale. His 1894 death is famed. His 1894 exile is famed.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Yuri Orlov, who died in 2020 at ninety-six, was both a serious physicist and a founder of the Soviet human rights movement. Svetlana Savranskaya and Tom Blanton compiled this memorial briefing book, number 724. Orlov founded the Moscow Helsinki Group, which monitored Soviet compliance with human rights promises.

He proposed glasnost, openness, almost fifteen years before Gorbachev made it policy. For that work he paid with prison and exile. The memorial builds on an earlier 2014 briefing book on Orlov, updated at his death. It preserves the record of a scientist who treated truth telling as a method, in physics and in politics alike.
nasa-tm-19720016358-preliminary-noise-te:
Meyer Reshotko, William A Olsen, and Robert G Dorsch of the Lewis Research Center reported these noise tests in March 1972, as NASA TM X-68032. They studied placing the engine over the wing of a short takeoff aircraft. The wing itself might then shield people below from jet noise. Cities near small airports needed such quiet designs. This first report covers the landing flap settings. The flaps sat at thirty and sixty degrees.

A small wing section model stood in for the full aircraft. Its chord measured about thirty two centimeters. Simulated engine exhaust flowed over the wing and flaps. The team recorded the sound the setup produced in each position. Engine over wing designs promised shielding plus blown lift. These early tests began measuring whether the promise held.
note-book-of-anton-chekhov:
Anton Chekhov's Note-Book came out in English in 1921, translated by S. S. Koteliansky and Leonard Woolf. A note up front explains the material: themes, thoughts, and fragments for works Chekhov meant to write. Sheets in a special cover held them among his papers. His wife kept the note-book itself.

Chekhov struck out any note once he used it in a work. He recopied most of the rest into a special copy book, which shows the worth he set on them. Diary pages from 1896 follow the notes. One tale tells of a poet who always spat at the University when his carriage passed it in Moscow.
rezanov: Gertrude Atherton's Rezanov (1906) romances a Russian chamberlain in early California. History meets passion on the frontier. The Tower library holds the full text. It dramatizes early San Francisco vividly. Love crosses empires boldly and blindly. The novel blends fact with feeling. Readers savored the exotic tale.
